title: Photography direction for an accounting firm
metaTitle: Accounting firm website photography with a point
excerpt: Accounting firm website photography should show who does the work and for whom. A skyline and the word excellence argue for a costume, not a person.
alt: Two people pointing at a laptop screen, one wearing a fitness band, a shared look at the work rather than a skyline standing in for the firm.
caption: Two people looking at one screen, the attention on the work. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should an accounting firm photograph?
faqs.answer: Photograph the people who do the work, at a real desk, with screens cleared of client data. Show a meeting a founder could actually sit in. Match the frames to the kinds of companies you serve. A skyline does not identify an accountant.

faqs.question: Why skip skylines and the word excellence in images?
faqs.answer: They reassure the firm and fail the founder. A calm expert is a person and a kind of company, both checkable on a call. A tower and a slogan look like every other finance costume, and they often cover the face that would have helped.

faqs.question: How should hero photos be prepared for the site?
faqs.answer: Export them at the size the layout uses, with width and height set so the page does not jump. Google's Core Web Vitals guidance asks for Largest Contentful Paint within 2.5 seconds and Cumulative Layout Shift under 0.1. One still photograph beats a carousel of cities.

markdown:
Accounting firm website photography should show who does the work and for whom. Choose frames that make that person and that kind of company easier to believe. Reject a skyline and the word excellence. The pictures are part of the argument. They are not a mood pasted under the headline.

A founder who needs a calm expert will look for a human and a recognizable kind of work before they finish the paragraph. Google's Core Web Vitals guidance treats the largest thing in view, often the hero image, as a loading measure, and asks that Largest Contentful Paint occur within 2.5 seconds. A heavy city photograph that arrives late has missed the moment the name needed it. Google's helpful-content guidance also asks for first-hand evidence. A tower you do not work in is not evidence that someone can close a month.

## The picture has to identify a person and a company type

Decide who and for whom before you book the photographer. If Mina closes the books for owner-led studios, the frames should help a studio founder imagine working with Mina. Her face, a normal desk, a laptop with the screen turned so no client file is visible. If the practice is clinics, the room should feel like a place a practitioner could talk about billings without a sales pitch. If the practice is shops with stock, one true detail beats a generic office: a simple table, paper, a person who looks uninterrupted.

One skyline cannot stand for every client type. It makes clinics, studios, and shops look like the same glass brand. Shoot for the people you name on the about page and the companies you name on the homepage. The services page can crop the same session. The homepage can use the clearest face, with the sentence beside it, not trapped under a dark gradient and a slogan.

Write the argument in a line the photographer can hold. "This frame should make a studio founder believe Mina is the person who will explain a number without drama." If you cannot write that line, you are shopping for prestige. Prestige photographs are cheap, and they all look like banks.

Only photograph staff who have agreed. A recognizable person matched to a bio is worth more than a silhouette against a window. A founder should connect the about page to the homepage without guessing which stock model you rented.

## What to put on the shot list

Bring a list. Do not improvise a brand out of the view from the lift.

- The person who leads the work you want, at their real desk, dressed as they dress for a client call. Face visible. Screen locked on a neutral page or turned away.
- A second frame of them in conversation at a table sized for two or three people, not a boardroom built for a keynote. The founder should see a meeting they could survive.
- Hands on a keyboard or a notebook, close enough to see work, far enough that no client name is readable. Stage a dummy file if you need paper. Never a live ledger.
- One detail that is true to the office: the window, the plant, the mug, the chair. Specific and plain.
- If the kind of company is part of the argument, a single environmental clue that does not mock the client. A clinic practice might show a quiet room. It should not show a fake patient.

Skip the skyline, the drone shot, the trading-floor glow, raining cash, a handshake on marble, and any word set in type across the photo, especially excellence. Those images say "finance" to a template and "not you" to a founder who wanted calm.

Tell everyone to clear screens before the shutter. A dashboard in the background is a confidentiality problem and a distraction. The photograph is not the proof page. The proof page can show a staged checkpoint. This session shows the humans.

Plan the crops. You need a face that survives a narrow phone column, a wider frame for a desktop hero that still keeps the sentence readable, and a small crop for the services block. Shoot the vertical on purpose. A beautiful horizontal that crops the head off will force the mobile page to lead with ceiling.

## A skyline and the word excellence are a costume

The skyline reassures partners that the firm looks established. Established, for this founder, is a named person who has done this kind of company. The tower pushes the name down the page. It also matches every other firm that bought the same view, including firms that do completely different work.

Excellence, burned into a photograph or sitting on a plaque you styled into the shot, cannot be checked. The founder cannot verify it in the ten seconds Nielsen Norman Group says they use to decide whether to stay. A face and a sentence can be checked on a call. Prefer those.

Glass lobbies and night cities have a second problem. They are loud. The buyer in this article wants a calm expert. A dramatic photograph argues with a quiet headline. If the picture is doing drama, the words about steadiness will lose.

A plain room is a better argument. It looks like a place where someone could say "this number is a timing issue" without performing. Hanabi's public project work, such as a store like Down the Cove, can show the thing being sold because the thing is public. What you are selling in the photograph is the person and the kind of attention. Show those. Leave the city on the map.

## Direction the photographer can follow

Give constraints, not adjectives. "Premium, elevated, dynamic" produces a skyline. Constraints produce the argument.

Name the order. The person who leads the featured work goes first, while everyone is fresh. What they wear is what they wear to a real call. For the about page, they look at the camera. For a work frame, they look at the page or the screen, with nothing sensitive showing. Shoot both.

Ban overlays in the notes. No slogan composited later, no skyline dropped behind a cut-out person, no gradient whose only job is to make a word like excellence legible. If the type is hard to read, the photograph is too busy or the type is in the wrong place. Move the type into the layout. Do not fog the room.

Choose frames against the sentence you wrote. Reject anything that could be a bank advertisement. Keep anything where a founder could say "that is the person from the bio" or "that looks like a studio's accountant, not a trading desk."

Keep color close to the room. A grade that turns the office gold or teal is another costume. Natural light, a face that reads on a phone outdoors, moderate contrast. If you lay the page out in Figma, drop the real frames in before you commit to a crop that collides with the headline.

Write the alt text while you still know the frame. "Mina Alvarez at a wooden desk, laptop open, screen turned away, window to the left." That describes the photograph. "Best accounting firm excellence" does not, and it stuffs a slogan into a picture a founder may not even see.

## Speed is part of the photograph

The hero is often the Largest Contentful Paint element. Google's good threshold is within 2.5 seconds of the page starting to load. Export the frame at the display size. A huge original of a skyline, scaled in the browser, taxes the founder for a costume.

Reserve the space. Cumulative Layout Shift should stay under 0.1, so the image needs a known width and height. A headline that jumps when the photo arrives is a miss during the only seconds you may get. Interaction to Next Paint should stay under 200 milliseconds. A carousel of cities, with dots a thumb must hunt, spends that budget on decoration. One still of the person is faster and more specific.

When you replace the hero, version the file so a cached skyline cannot sit beside a new sentence about a named person. The picture and the copy ship together.

Reduced motion still applies if you were tempted to pan across the city. Offer the still. Some people get ill from the pan, and the person in the frame did not need to move to be credible.

## Where each frame goes

The homepage gets one clear argument: the person, the company type in text, the booking. Not a slideshow of the district.

The services page gets a crop that matches the job only if it still shows a human. Monthly books can be the desk. A cleanup can be the same person with the dummy checklist, if you are careful. Do not assign a stock city to each service in the name of variety.

The about page gets faces that match names. The contact page gets the person who replies, or the room the video call represents, so booking feels continuous. Proof pages get a staged method image, never a client dashboard.

Captions can carry a little of the argument. "Mina closes the month for owner-led studios." Alt text stays a description of the frame. If the photograph is from a library, the caption should not pretend it is your office.

## Review the set before it is live

Lay the frames in order with the sentences hidden. Ask someone outside the firm: who works here, and for what kind of company? If they say "a big finance brand" or "a city," the skyline won. If they describe a person at a desk, you are close. Then show the sentence. Picture and sentence should agree.

Check the phone crop. The face has to remain a face. The booking and the name have to remain readable. If the only way to read the name is to hide the photograph, change the frame or the layout.

The next failure is usually the phone page itself. A wide composition that felt balanced can stack the skyline first and push the person below the fold. Read [how the mobile visit should be built](/blog/the-mobile-visit-for-an-accounting-firm) before you approve a crop that only works on a monitor.

When you want a second opinion on whether the pictures and the people agree, [book an intro call with Hanabi](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the shot list and one frame you are unsure about.
